posts.title: One marked piece at the end of Thursday
posts.excerpt: A teaching week at Hibana College keeps the same order of days, and it closes when one marked piece goes on the review rack.
posts.content:
A teaching week on the Six-Month Course has a fixed order. Monday is demonstration and drawing. Tuesday and Wednesday are spent in the booth. Thursday morning is cut, bend and review. Thursday afternoon is clean down, and the drawing for the week after. The week stops there. Friday is free on purpose, because many students keep a part-time job, and the college does not put teaching on the day that job needs. Day hours are 8:30 to 16:30, with seven taught hours inside them. The shape holds for all 26 weeks.

What closes the week is one marked piece on the review rack. Not a pile of attempts, and not a grade posted later from an office. The piece is the week's work, marked and left where the cohort can see it. Across the room, that becomes a row of finished practice pieces. The mark is how this workshop reads the week. It is not a qualification, and it is not a statement about employment. Students who want a certificate from some other body will not find one issued here under another name.

The piece itself changes with the month. In month 1, after PPE, fume, grinding, cutting and reading a drawing, it is a squared, cut and filed steel block. In month 2 it is a T-joint that passes a break test, from flat and horizontal MIG fillets. In month 3 it is a vertical-up fillet plate, from stick in the vertical and overhead. In month 4 it is a clean stainless butt joint, from TIG torch and filler control on steel and stainless. In month 5 it is a welded steel gate frame, after layout, cutting, fit-up and distortion. In month 6 the bench gives up a test plate set and an inspector's report. A visiting independent inspector sees those plates. The same month includes two weeks on placement in a local shop.

Thursday morning is when a joint from the booth gets looked at properly. A fillet may be cut or bent. The break test in month 2 is there so the weld is judged by whether it holds, not only by the look of the ripples. Later months ask whether a frame stayed square, or whether the stainless joint is clean. The afternoon is then plain work that still counts as taught time: clean the booth down, and take the next drawing. Monday's demonstration has something to stand on because Thursday was finished, not because anyone stayed late on Friday.

People arrive at this week from other jobs. Marit Solberg founded Hibana College in 2011 after leaving shipyard fitting, to teach adults who had never held a torch. The application is one page, and it does not ask for experience. The usual first visit is Open Bench, free, on the first Saturday of the month, from 10:00 to 13:00, trying a torch under supervision. Then the application, then a bench talk of 30 minutes with Claire Dubois and one instructor. On day one, a $500 deposit secures a booth. Helmet, jacket, gloves and boots are issued that first morning.

Three cohorts start each year, on 11 January, 3 May and 6 September. Each one is 12 students and two instructors, a ratio of 1:6, for 728 hours, at $9,800. The $500 deposit is the first payment. Six monthly payments of $1,550 make up the rest. The workshop at 27 Slipway Road, Port Aldren, has 24 booths. Samir Haddad, the workshop and safety officer, gives the first-day briefing before anyone works alone in one of them.

The office answers questions about the next start from Monday to Friday, 9:00 to 17:00, at hello@hibanacollege.example or on +1 555 0142. We teach the trade and arrange the placement. We cannot promise a job or a test result. The marked piece on the rack is a record of one week in this workshop. It says what the hands did between Monday's drawing and Thursday's review. It does not say where someone will be working when the 26 weeks are over.
